questions.question: A point charge $(q)$ is placed in an electric field of magnitude $E$. The force experienced by the charge will be:
questions.answer:
**(A) $qE$**

By the definition of electric field intensity, $\vec E=\vec F/q$, hence

$$\vec F=q\vec E\quad\Rightarrow\quad F=qE$$

The force acts along the field if $q$ is positive and opposite to it if $q$ is negative.

questions.question: According to Biot–Savart law magnetic field at a point due to current carrying element depends on distance of a point from current element as:
questions.answer:
**(D) $B\propto\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$**

Biot–Savart law:

$$d\vec B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec l\times\hat r}{r^{2}}$$

so for a given current element and direction, $dB\propto\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$ — an inverse-square dependence, exactly like Coulomb's law.

questions.question: Which phenomenon shows that light is a transverse wave?
questions.answer:
**(C) Polarisation**

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because polarisation restricts the vibration to one plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Diffraction and interference occur for longitudinal waves as well (e.g. sound), so they do not prove the transverse nature of light.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Wavelength of matter wave is given by:
questions.answer:
**(A) $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}$**

By de Broglie's hypothesis every moving particle of momentum $p$ has an associated wave of wavelength

$$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{mv}$$

where $h$ is Planck's constant.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: With rise in temperature resistivity of an intrinsic semiconductor:
questions.answer:
**(B) decreases**

In a semiconductor the number density of charge carriers increases very rapidly with temperature (many more electron–hole pairs are generated), and this increase far outweighs the reduction in relaxation time.

$$\rho=\frac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}\quad\text{and}\quad n\ \text{increases rapidly with}\ T$$

Hence resistivity (and resistance) of an intrinsic semiconductor decreases with rise in temperature — it has a negative temperature coefficient.

questions.question: Write down the basic properties of electric charge.
questions.answer:
**1. Conservation of charge:** The total charge of an isolated system remains constant. Charge can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transferred from one body to another. For an isolated system of bodies, $\sum q=0$ initially and finally.

**2. Additivity of charge:** Total charge on a system is the algebraic sum of the charges on its individual bodies, taking signs into account. If a system contains charges $q_1,q_2,-q_3$, then $Q=q_1+q_2-q_3$. Charges are scalars and add algebraically.

**3. Quantisation of charge:** The total charge on a body is always an integral multiple of the elementary charge $e$:

$$q=\pm ne,\qquad n=1,2,3,\dots,\quad e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$$

**4. Charge is unaffected by motion:** The charge on a body is the same whether it is at rest or in motion — charge is a relativistic invariant. (Charge at rest = charge in motion.)

**5. Interaction of charges:** Like charges repel and unlike charges attract each other, the force between two point charges in vacuum being $F=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}}$.

questions.question: What do you understand by drift velocity and mobility?
questions.answer:
**Drift velocity ($v_d$):** It is the average velocity acquired by the free electrons of a conductor in the direction opposite to the applied electric field.

When a field $\vec E$ is applied, each electron experiences a force and its velocity changes randomly between collisions. The average velocity over a large number of electrons is

$$\vec v_d=-\frac{e\vec E}{m}\tau$$

where $m$ is the electron mass and $\tau$ the relaxation time (= mean free path / rms speed of electrons). Typically $v_d\sim10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$ — very small compared with the thermal speeds.

**Relaxation time:** $\tau=\dfrac{\text{mean free path}}{\text{root mean square velocity of electrons}}$.

**Mobility ($\mu$):** It is the drift velocity acquired per unit electric field:

$$\mu=\frac{v_d}{E}=\frac{e\tau}{m}$$

Its SI unit is m$^{2}$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. Larger mobility means the charge carrier responds more readily to the field, and conductivity is $\sigma=ne\mu$.

questions.question: Show that in parallel grouping of a number of cells the value of current will be same as that due to a single cell when internal resistance of cell is negligible in comparison to external resistance in circuit.
questions.answer:
Consider $m$ identical cells, each of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$, connected in parallel across an external resistance $R$.

**Parallel grouping:** In this combination the emfs of all cells are equal and act in the same sense, so the net emf of the combination is just that of a single cell, $\varepsilon$. The internal resistances are in parallel, so the total internal resistance is $r/m$.

Hence the current is

$$I=\frac{\varepsilon}{R+\dfrac{r}{m}}$$

**When $r\ll R$** so that the internal resistance is negligible compared with the external resistance,

$$I=\frac{\varepsilon}{R+\dfrac{r}{m}}\approx\frac{\varepsilon}{R}$$

which is exactly the current produced by a single cell of emf $\varepsilon$ across $R$ (for one cell, $I=\varepsilon/(R+r)\approx\varepsilon/R$).

Thus, when the internal resistance is negligible compared with the external resistance, parallel grouping gives no gain in current — it merely increases the current capacity (life) of the battery.

questions.question: Using Ampere's circuital law find magnetic field at a point due to very long current carrying straight wire, when point is outside the wire.
questions.answer:
Let a very long straight wire carry a current $I$. Let $P$ be a point at a perpendicular distance $r$ from the wire; $PO=r$.

**Step 1 — Amperian loop.** Imagine a circle of radius $r$ with the wire as its axis, passing through $P$ and lying in a plane perpendicular to the wire. By symmetry, the magnetic field has the same magnitude $B$ at every point of this circle and is everywhere tangential to it.

**Step 2 — Apply Ampere's circuital law:**

$$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$$

Since $\vec B\parallel d\vec l$ at every point of the circle,

$$B\oint dl=\mu_0 I$$

**Step 3.** The circumference of the circle is $2\pi r$, so

$$B\,(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I$$

$$\boxed{B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}}$$

Thus the field falls off as $1/r$ and its direction is given by the right-hand grip rule.

questions.question: Write down Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction.
questions.answer:
**First law:** Whenever the magnetic lines of force passing through a closed circuit (coil) change, an emf is induced in the circuit, and it lasts only so long as the change continues.

- If the flux linked with a coil changes, an induced emf appears in the coil.
- The induced emf disappears as soon as the change in flux stops.

**Second law:** The magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit, and to the number of turns in the coil.

$$\varepsilon=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$

where $N$ is the number of turns and $d\Phi/dt$ the rate of change of flux through one turn. The negative sign (Lenz's law) shows that the induced emf opposes the change in flux.

**Corollary:** If the flux changes from $\Phi_1$ to $\Phi_2$ in time $\Delta t$, then $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Phi_2-\Phi_1}{\Delta t}$, and the induced charge is $q=\dfrac{N(\Phi_1-\Phi_2)}{R}$.

questions.question: Find the relation between critical angle and refractive index.
questions.answer:
When light passes from a denser medium into a rarer medium it bends away from the normal. As the angle of incidence is increased, the angle of refraction increases and at a certain stage it becomes $90^\circ$.

The **critical angle** $C$ is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is $90^\circ$.

Let $n_d$ be the refractive index of the denser medium and $n_r$ that of the rarer medium. By Snell's law, at the critical angle,

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{n_r}{n_d}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{\sin C}{\sin90^\circ}=\frac{n_r}{n_d}$$

Since $\sin90^\circ=1$,

$$\sin C=\frac{n_r}{n_d}$$

If the rarer medium is air ($n_r=1$) and $n=n_d$ is the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to air, then

$$\boxed{\sin C=\frac{1}{n}}$$

So $n=\dfrac{1}{\sin C}=\operatorname{cosec}C$. For glass ($n=1.5$), $C\approx41.8^\circ$.

questions.question: Explain the principle of MODEM in brief.
questions.answer:
A **modem** (MOdulator–DEModulator) is a device which transfers data from one computer to another at a distant place over a communication link such as a telephone line.

**Principle:** It acts both as a modulator and as a demodulator — the name is made from these two functions.

- **At the transmitting end** the modem accepts the digital data from the computer and converts it into analog signals suitable for modulating a carrier wave, which can then travel over the communication network.
- **At the receiving end** the modem demodulates the received carrier wave and recovers the original digital data.

$$\text{Computer}\to\text{Modulator}\to\text{Channel}\to\text{Demodulator}\to\text{Computer}$$

Modems are classified according to their transmission speed (bits per second). Computer–internet connection is the commonest example of modem use.

questions.question: Calculate the equivalent resistance of the network between points $X$ and $Y$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — Identify the arms.** The network may be redrawn as a quadrilateral between the terminals $X$ and $Y$ with the five resistances:

- $X\to a$: $15\ \Omega$
- $a\to b$: $40\ \Omega$ (the middle arm)
- $b\to Y$: $30\ \Omega$
- $X\to b$: $30\ \Omega$ (upper path)
- $a\to Y$: $15\ \Omega$ (lower path)

**Step 2 — Test the Wheatstone balance.**

$$\frac{R_{Xa}}{R_{Xb}}=\frac{15}{30}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad \frac{R_{aY}}{R_{bY}}=\frac{15}{30}=\frac{1}{2}$$

Since $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{R}{S}$, the bridge is **balanced**: the potentials of $a$ and $b$ are equal, so no current flows through the $40\ \Omega$ resistance and it may be removed.

**Step 3 — Series combinations.**

$$R_1=15+15=30\ \Omega\quad(\text{path }X\to a\to Y)$$

$$R_2=30+30=60\ \Omega\quad(\text{path }X\to b\to Y)$$

**Step 4 — Parallel combination.** These two paths are in parallel between $X$ and $Y$:

$$\frac{1}{R_{XY}}=\frac{1}{30}+\frac{1}{60}=\frac{2+1}{60}=\frac{3}{60}=\frac{1}{20}$$

$$\boxed{R_{XY}=20\ \Omega}$$

questions.question: What do you understand by self and mutual induction? Define mutual inductance.
questions.answer:
**Self induction:** The phenomenon according to which an opposing emf is induced in a coil as a result of a change of current (and hence of magnetic flux) linked with the coil itself is called self induction.

$$\varepsilon=-L\frac{dI}{dt}$$

where $L$ is the **coefficient of self inductance** (or simply inductance) of the coil: it is the flux linked with the coil per unit current through it, $L=\Phi/I$. Its SI unit is the henry (H).

**Mutual induction:** The phenomenon according to which an opposing emf is induced in a coil as a result of a change of current (or of magnetic flux) linked with a neighbouring coil is called mutual induction.

$$\varepsilon_2=-M\frac{dI_1}{dt}$$

**Definition of mutual inductance ($M$):** The mutual inductance of two coils is the magnetic flux linked with one coil per unit current flowing in the other coil:

$$M=\frac{\Phi_2}{I_1}=\frac{\Phi_1}{I_2}$$

Equivalently, it is numerically equal to the emf induced in one coil when the current in the other coil changes at the rate of 1 A s$^{-1}$. Its SI unit is also the henry (H). For two coils wound on a common core, $M=K\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, where $K$ is the coupling coefficient ($0\le K\le1$).

Mutual inductance depends on the geometry of the coils, their number of turns, their separation and the nature of the core.

questions.question: An emf of 230 volts with frequency 50 Hz is applied to a circuit containing a capacitor of capacitance $5\ \mu$F in series with resistance of $1000$ ohm. Find the rate at which energy (power) is dissipated in the circuit.
questions.answer:
Given: $\varepsilon=230$ V, $f=50$ Hz, $C=5\ \mu$F $=5\times10^{-6}$ F, $R=1000\ \Omega$.

**Step 1 — Capacitive reactance.**

$$X_C=\frac{1}{2\pi fC}=\frac{1}{2\times3.14\times50\times5\times10^{-6}}=\frac{1}{1.571\times10^{-3}}=636.6\ \Omega$$

**Step 2 — Impedance of the series RC circuit.**

$$Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+X_C^{2}}=\sqrt{(1000)^{2}+(636.6)^{2}}=\sqrt{10^{6}+4.05\times10^{5}}=1185\ \Omega$$

**Step 3 — rms current.**

$$I_{\text{rms}}=\frac{\varepsilon_{\text{rms}}}{Z}=\frac{230}{1185}=0.194\ \text{A}$$

**Step 4 — Power dissipated.** Only the resistance dissipates power (the capacitor stores and returns energy, average power in it being zero for a full cycle):

$$P=I_{\text{rms}}^{2}R=(0.194)^{2}\times1000=0.0376\times1000$$

$$\boxed{P\approx37.6\ \text{W}}$$

(The energy stored in the capacitor at the peak voltage is only $U=\tfrac12CV^{2}=\tfrac12\times5\times10^{-6}\times(230)^2=0.132$ J; it is not dissipated but exchanged with the source.)

questions.question: Write four characteristics of electromagnetic waves. Write the expression for the velocity of electromagnetic waves in terms of permittivity and magnetic permeability of free space.
questions.answer:
**Characteristics of electromagnetic waves:**

1. **No material medium needed:** Electromagnetic waves do not require any medium for their propagation; they can travel through vacuum.
2. **Transverse nature:** They are transverse — the electric field $\vec E$ and magnetic field $\vec B$ are mutually perpendicular and both are perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
3. **Speed in free space:**

$$c_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$$

where $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space and $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}$ C$^{2}$ N$^{-1}$ m$^{-2}$ is the permittivity of free space. Numerically $c_0=3\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$.
4. **Relation between the fields:** In vacuum $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are related by

$$c_0=\frac{E_0}{B_0}$$

where $E_0$ and $B_0$ are the amplitudes of the electric and magnetic fields. The energy is shared equally between the two fields.

5. The electric field vector $\vec E$ is mainly responsible for the optical effects of an electromagnetic wave.
6. They carry energy and momentum, are unaffected by electric and magnetic fields, and show reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation.

questions.question: Explain the reddish appearance of sky at sunrise and sunset.
questions.answer:
At sunrise and sunset the sun is near the horizon, so its rays have to travel a much longer path through the atmosphere to reach the observer than at noon.

According to Rayleigh's law, the intensity of the light scattered by molecules of air is

$$I\propto\frac{1}{\lambda^{4}}$$

so blue light ($\lambda$ small) is scattered far more strongly than red light ($\lambda$ large).

Along the long path, most of the blue and shorter wavelengths are scattered out of the direct beam. Only the longer wavelengths — orange and red — survive along the line of sight and reach our eyes directly from the sun.

Hence the sun appears reddish/orange at sunrise and sunset.

questions.topic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
questions.question: A short sighted person uses lens for observing object at a distance of 200 cm but he can see an object at a distance of 20 cm without any use of lens. Find the focal length and nature of correcting lens required. Also find the power of correcting lens.
questions.answer:
A short-sighted (myopic) person can see objects clearly only up to his far point. Here that far point is at $20$ cm, and the object he wants to see lies at $200$ cm.

The correcting lens must form the virtual image of the distant object at the far point, so using the sign convention (distances measured from the lens, against the incident light being negative):

$$u=-200\ \text{cm},\qquad v=-20\ \text{cm}$$

By the lens formula,

$$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{-20}-\frac{1}{-200}=\frac{-10+1}{200}=\frac{-9}{200}$$

$$f=-\frac{200}{9}=-22.2\ \text{cm}$$

**Nature:** $f$ is negative, so the lens must be **concave (diverging)**.

**Power:**

$$P=\frac{1}{f\ (\text{in metre})}=\frac{1}{-0.222}=-4.5\ \text{D}$$

So a concave lens of focal length $22.2$ cm and power $-4.5$ dioptre is required.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: The work function of a metal surface is $1.2$ eV. Calculate the kinetic energy of the fastest and slowest photoelectrons and the retarding potential when light of frequency $5.5\times10^{14}$ Hz falls on the surface. ($h=6.62\times10^{-34}$ J s)
questions.answer:
Given: $\phi_0=1.2$ eV $=1.2\times1.6\times10^{-19}=1.92\times10^{-19}$ J, $\nu=5.5\times10^{14}$ Hz, $h=6.62\times10^{-34}$ J s.

**Step 1 — Energy of the incident photon.**

$$E=h\nu=6.62\times10^{-34}\times5.5\times10^{14}=3.64\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

**Step 2 — Kinetic energy of the fastest photoelectron** (Einstein's equation):

$$K_{\max}=h\nu-\phi_0=(3.64-1.92)\times10^{-19}$$

$$K_{\max}=1.72\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}=\frac{1.72\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=1.08\ \text{eV}$$

**Step 3 — Kinetic energy of the slowest photoelectron:** The slowest electrons are those emitted from the surface with just enough energy to escape, so

$$K_{\min}=0$$

**Step 4 — Retarding (stopping) potential:**

$$eV_0=K_{\max}\ \Rightarrow\ V_0=\frac{1.72\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=1.08\ \text{V}$$

**Answer:** $K_{\max}=1.72\times10^{-19}$ J $\approx1.08$ eV, $K_{\min}=0$, retarding potential $V_0\approx1.08$ V.

questions.question: Write down the radioactive decay law. Prove that the expression of half-life time is given by $T=\dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$, where $\lambda$ is decay constant.
questions.answer:
**Radioactive decay law:** The rate of decay of radioactive nuclei is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present at that instant:

$$\frac{dN}{dt}=-\lambda N$$

where $\lambda$ is the decay constant (probability of decay per nucleus per unit time).

Integrating with $N=N_0$ at $t=0$:

$$\int\frac{dN}{N}=-\lambda\int dt\ \Rightarrow\ \ln N=-\lambda t+\text{const}$$

$$\boxed{N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}}$$

**Half-life ($T$):** It is the time in which half the number of atoms present initially in a sample decays, i.e. the number of undecayed atoms becomes $N_0/2$.

Putting $N=N_0/2$ at $t=T$:

$$\frac{N_0}{2}=N_0e^{-\lambda T}\ \Rightarrow\ e^{-\lambda T}=\frac{1}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ e^{\lambda T}=2$$

Taking logarithms of both sides,

$$\lambda T=\ln 2=2.303\log_{10}2$$

$$T=\frac{\ln2}{\lambda}=\frac{2.303\times0.3010}{\lambda}=\frac{0.693}{\lambda}$$

$$\boxed{T=\frac{0.693}{\lambda}}$$

Thus half-life is inversely proportional to the decay constant. In $n$ half-lives, $N=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n}$.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: How a NAND gate can be used to work as OR, AND and NOT gate?
questions.answer:
The NAND gate is a **universal gate** — every other logic gate can be built from NAND gates alone. Its output is $Y=\overline{A\cdot B}$.

**1. NAND as NOT gate:** Tie both inputs of the NAND gate together to the same input $A$:

$$Y=\overline{A\cdot A}=\bar A$$

so a single NAND with shorted inputs acts as an inverter (NOT).

**2. NAND as AND gate:** Pass the output of a NAND gate through a NAND gate used as an inverter:

$$Y=\overline{\overline{A\cdot B}}=A\cdot B$$

So AND $=$ NAND followed by NOT.

**3. NAND as OR gate:** First invert $A$ and $B$ separately using two NAND gates with their inputs shorted, then NAND the two inverted outputs:

$$Y=\overline{\bar A\cdot\bar B}=\bar A+\bar B\ \text{ complemented}\ =A+B$$

that is, $Y=A+B$ by De Morgan's theorem.

Thus NAND alone can realise NOT, AND and OR, and hence any logic circuit.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: What is Zener diode? How can it be used as voltage regulator?
questions.answer:
**Zener diode:** A Zener diode is a specially designed junction diode which is heavily doped so that it can operate in the region of reverse breakdown voltage without being damaged. In reverse bias beyond the Zener voltage $V_Z$ its current increases very rapidly while the voltage across it stays almost constant. Its symbol is drawn with the cathode bar bent at both ends.

**Zener diode as a voltage regulator:**

Voltage regulation is the ability of a circuit to maintain a constant output voltage even when the input voltage or the load current varies.

- The Zener diode is connected in **reverse bias** across the varying input $V_{in}$, through a series resistance $R$.
- The load resistance $R_L$ is connected in parallel with the Zener diode, so the output voltage is the Zener voltage $V_{out}=V_Z$.
- When the input voltage rises, the extra voltage is dropped across the series resistance $R$ and the Zener current increases; the voltage across the diode (and hence across the load) stays at $V_Z$.

$$I=I_Z+I_L,\qquad V_{in}=IR+V_Z$$

- If the load current $I_L$ increases, $I_Z$ decreases by the same amount, keeping $I$ and hence the drop across $R$ unchanged; $V_{out}$ remains $V_Z$.

Thus the output voltage is stabilised at the Zener breakdown voltage, and the series resistance absorbs the excess voltage.

questions.question: Using Bohr's atomic model find the wave number of Lyman series and Balmer series in hydrogen spectra.
questions.answer:
According to Bohr's theory, when an electron jumps from an orbit of quantum number $n_i$ to an orbit of lower quantum number $n_f$, the wave number of the emitted radiation is

$$\bar\nu=\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$$

where $R=1.097\times10^{7}$ m$^{-1}$ is the Rydberg constant.

**1. Lyman series** — transitions ending on the first orbit ($n_f=1$), $n_i=2,3,4,\dots$

$$\bar\nu=\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right),\qquad n_i=2,3,4,\dots$$

- Longest wavelength ($n_i=2$):

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_{\max}}=R\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{3R}{4}\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_{\max}=\frac{4}{3R}=\frac{4}{3\times1.097\times10^{7}}=1.215\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=1215\ \text{Å}$$

- Shortest wavelength (series limit, $n_i=\infty$):

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}}=R\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_{\min}=\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{1.097\times10^{7}}=9.12\times10^{-8}\ \text{m}=912\ \text{Å}$$

The Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet region.

**2. Balmer series** — transitions ending on the second orbit ($n_f=2$), $n_i=3,4,5,\dots$

$$\bar\nu=\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right),\qquad n_i=3,4,5,\dots$$

- Longest wavelength ($n_i=3$):

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_{\max}}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right)=\frac{5R}{36}\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_{\max}=\frac{36}{5R}=\frac{36}{5\times1.097\times10^{7}}=6.56\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=6563\ \text{Å}$$

- Shortest wavelength (series limit, $n_i=\infty$):

$$\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}-0\right)=\frac{R}{4}\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_{\min}=\frac{4}{R}=\frac{4}{1.097\times10^{7}}=3.65\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=3646\ \text{Å}$$

The Balmer series lies in the visible region; its first line $H_\alpha$ is at $6563$ Å, then $H_\beta$, $H_\gamma$, …

questions.topic: Communication Systems — Sky and Space Wave Propagation
questions.question: Discuss the different modes of sky and space wave propagation in brief.
questions.answer:
**Sky wave propagation:** These are waves radiated upward at large angles by the antenna which, after reflection from the ionosphere (or a satellite), reach the receiving antenna.

The frequency range used for sky wave propagation by ionospheric reflection is from a few MHz up to about $30$ MHz. The refractive index of the ionised layers depends on frequency as

$$\mu=\sqrt{1-\frac{81}{f^{2}}}$$

which shows that reflection occurs only below a certain critical frequency; above it the wave escapes through the ionosphere. Sky waves can therefore cover very long distances (thousands of km) beyond the horizon, and are used for short-wave radio broadcast.

The highest frequency reflected from the earth is $f_c=9\sqrt{n_{\max}}$ for a vertically directed beam, where $n_{\max}$ is the maximum ion density.

**Space wave propagation:** Space waves are limited to the troposphere region of the atmosphere and have two components:

- **Direct waves** — travel directly from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna.
- **Reflected (ground) waves** — travel from the transmitting antenna to the earth's surface and are then reflected to the receiving antenna.

Space waves are used for (1) line-of-sight communication and (2) satellite communication. Their range is limited by the curvature of the earth and by the height of the antenna: $d=\sqrt{2Rh_T}+\sqrt{2Rh_R}$.

questions.question: Find the energy stored in a capacitor. Using it find the energy density of a parallel plate capacitor.
questions.answer:
**Energy stored in a charged capacitor:**

When a capacitor is charged by a battery, work is done by the battery at the expense of its chemical energy; this work is stored in the capacitor as electrostatic potential energy.

Let the capacitor have capacitance $C$ and let its instantaneous charge be $q$, so the potential difference across it is $V=q/C$. The work done in giving it an additional infinitesimal charge $dq$ is

$$dW=V\,dq=\frac{q}{C}\,dq$$

The total work done in charging it from $0$ to $Q$ is therefore

$$W=\int_0^{Q}\frac{q}{C}\,dq=\frac{1}{C}\left[\frac{q^{2}}{2}\right]_0^{Q}=\frac{1}{C}\left(\frac{Q^{2}}{2}-0\right)=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C}$$

This work is stored as electrostatic potential energy, so with $Q=CV$,

$$\boxed{U=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C}=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}=\frac{1}{2}QV}$$

**Energy density of a parallel plate capacitor:**

For a parallel plate capacitor of plate area $A$ and separation $d$ filled with a dielectric of constant $K$,

$$C=\frac{K\varepsilon_0A}{d}$$

If $\sigma$ is the surface charge density, the field between the plates is

$$E=\frac{\sigma}{K\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ \sigma=K\varepsilon_0E$$

so the charge on each plate is $Q=\sigma A=K\varepsilon_0EA$, and

$$U=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C}=\frac{(K\varepsilon_0EA)^{2}}{2\,(K\varepsilon_0A/d)}=\frac{1}{2}K\varepsilon_0E^{2}Ad$$

But $Ad=\tau$, the volume of the space between the plates. Hence

$$U=\frac{1}{2}K\varepsilon_0E^{2}\,\tau$$

The electrostatic energy per unit volume (energy density) is

$$\boxed{u_E=\frac{U}{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}K\varepsilon_0E^{2}}$$

In air or free space ($K=1$), $u_E=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^{2}$. Thus the energy is stored in the electric field itself.

questions.question: Using Gauss theorem find the electric field intensity at a point due to a uniformly charged spherical shell.
questions.answer:
Consider a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius $R$ carrying a total charge $+q$, with its centre at $O$. We find the field at a point $P$ at distance $r$ from $O$, in the three regions.

**1. Point outside the shell ($r>R$):**

Draw a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ through $P$, concentric with the shell. By symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and has the same magnitude everywhere on it. Then

$$\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec S=E\,(4\pi r^{2})=\frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$$

$$\boxed{E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^{2}}}$$

The shell behaves as if all its charge were concentrated at its centre.

**2. Point on the surface ($r=R$):**

$$E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{R^{2}}$$

**3. Point inside the shell ($r<R$):**

The Gaussian surface now lies entirely inside the shell and encloses no charge, $q_{\text{enclosed}}=0$. Hence

$$E\,(4\pi r^{2})=0\ \Rightarrow\ E=0$$

**Result:** The field is zero everywhere inside a uniformly charged spherical shell, and outside it the shell behaves like a point charge at its centre. The potential inside is constant and equal to $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{R}$.

questions.topic: Bar Magnet — Field on Axis and Equator
questions.question: Find the magnetic field due to a bar magnet at a point along its axis and perpendicular to its axis.
questions.answer:
Let the bar magnet have length $2l$, pole strength $m$, and magnetic moment $M=m\times2l$. Let $O$ be its centre.

**(i) Field at a point on the axial (end-on) position** at distance $d$ from $O$:

The field due to the north pole (at distance $d-l$) and due to the south pole (at distance $d+l$) are both along $\vec{OP}$ and $\vec{PO}$ respectively:

$$B_N=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{(d-l)^{2}}\ \text{along } \vec{OP},\qquad B_S=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{(d+l)^{2}}\ \text{along } \vec{PO}$$

Since $B_N>B_S$, the resultant is

$$B=B_N-B_S=\frac{\mu_0m}{4\pi}\left[\frac{1}{(d-l)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(d+l)^{2}}\right]$$

$$=\frac{\mu_0m}{4\pi}\cdot\frac{4ld}{(d^{2}-l^{2})^{2}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2Md}{(d^{2}-l^{2})^{2}}$$

$$\boxed{B_{\text{axial}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2Md}{(d^{2}-l^{2})^{2}}}$$

For a short magnet ($d\gg l$): $B_{\text{axial}}\approx\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2M}{d^{3}}$.

**(ii) Field at a point on the broadside-on (equatorial) position** at distance $d$ from $O$:

Here the two field vectors have equal magnitudes

$$B_N=B_S=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{(d^{2}+l^{2})}$$

Their components along $\vec{OP}$ cancel and their components perpendicular to $\vec{OP}$ (along $\vec{PA}$) add:

$$B=B_N\cos\theta+B_S\cos\theta=2B_N\cos\theta$$

with $\cos\theta=\dfrac{l}{\sqrt{d^{2}+l^{2}}}$:

$$B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{(d^{2}+l^{2})}\cdot\frac{l}{\sqrt{d^{2}+l^{2}}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2ml}{(d^{2}+l^{2})^{3/2}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{M}{(d^{2}+l^{2})^{3/2}}$$

$$\boxed{B_{\text{equatorial}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{M}{(d^{2}+l^{2})^{3/2}}}$$

For a short magnet, $B_{\text{equatorial}}\approx\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{M}{d^{3}}$, which is half the axial field at the same distance.

questions.question: Find the force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field; using it find the force between two parallel current-carrying wires.
questions.answer:
**Force on a conductor in a uniform magnetic field:**

A conductor of length $L$ carrying current $I$ in a magnetic field $\vec B$ experiences a force on each charge carrier; the force on the whole conductor is

$$\vec F=I\,(\vec L\times\vec B)\quad\Rightarrow\quad F=BIL\sin\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the conductor and the field. The force is maximum when $\theta=90^\circ$ and zero when the conductor is parallel to $\vec B$.

**Force between two parallel wires:**

Consider two long parallel conductors $PQ$ and $RS$, separated by a distance $r$, carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ in the same direction.

The field produced by $PQ$ at the location of $RS$ is

$$B_1=\frac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi r}$$

By Maxwell's right-hand rule its direction is perpendicular to the plane of the wires. Each element of $RS$ of length $\Delta L$ therefore carries current perpendicular to $B_1$, and experiences a force

$$\Delta F=B_1I_2\Delta L\sin90^\circ=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}\Delta L$$

Hence the total force on a length $L$ of the conductor is

$$F=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}L$$

and the force per unit length is

$$\boxed{f=\frac{F}{L}=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}}$$

**Direction:** By Fleming's left-hand rule the force on $RS$ is towards $PQ$ — i.e. **parallel currents attract**. If the currents are in opposite directions the force is **repulsive**. The magnitude in each case is the same, in accordance with Newton's third law.

questions.question: Write down the Huygens principle. Using Huygens principle prove the laws of reflection and refraction of light.
questions.answer:
**Huygens' principle:**

1. Every point of a wavefront acts as a fresh source of secondary disturbances, called secondary wavelets, which spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave in that medium.
2. The envelope of all these secondary wavelets at a given instant gives the new position (new wavefront) of the wave at that instant.

The locus of all particles of a medium vibrating in the same phase is called a wavefront — spherical for a point source, cylindrical for a line source and plane for a distant source.

**Law of reflection:**

Let $XY$ be a reflecting surface and $AB$ a plane wavefront incident obliquely on it, striking it first at $A$ at time $t=0$. In time $t$ the disturbance at $B$ travels to $C$ with speed $v$, so $BC=vt$. Meanwhile, secondary wavelets from $A$ travel a distance $vt$ in the first medium, giving a sphere of radius $vt$. Draw the tangent $CD$ from $C$ to this sphere; then $CD$ is the reflected wavefront.

In right triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$: $AC$ is common and $AD=BC=vt$ (both equal to the distance travelled in the same time). Hence the triangles are congruent, so

$$\angle BAC=\angle DCA$$

Since $\angle i=\angle BAC$ and $\angle r=\angle DCA$ (angles between the wavefronts and the surface equal the angles between the corresponding rays and the normal),

$$\boxed{\angle i=\angle r}$$

and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.

**Law of refraction (Snell's law):**

Let $AB$ be a plane wavefront in a medium of refractive index $n_1$, incident on the boundary $XY$ separating it from a medium of refractive index $n_2$. Let $A$ touch the surface at $t=0$; the disturbance at $B$ reaches $C$ in time $t$, so $BC=v_1t$ in the first medium. In the same interval, secondary wavelets from $A$ travel in the second medium a distance $AD=v_2t$.

Draw the tangent $CD$ from $C$ to the sphere of radius $AD$; $CD$ is the refracted wavefront. In right triangles $ABC$ and $ACD$:

$$\sin i=\frac{BC}{AC}=\frac{v_1t}{AC},\qquad \sin r=\frac{AD}{AC}=\frac{v_2t}{AC}$$

Dividing,

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{v_1}{v_2}$$

Since $v_1=c/n_1$ and $v_2=c/n_2$,

$$\boxed{\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{n_2}{n_1}=n_{21}}$$

which is Snell's law; the incident ray, refracted ray and normal are coplanar.

questions.question: Establish lens maker formula $\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Consider a thin lens of refractive index $n_2$ (denoted $\mu_2$) placed in a medium of refractive index $n_1$ ($\mu_1$). Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the poles of its two spherical surfaces $AP_1B$ and $AP_2B$, with centres of curvature $C_1$ and $C_2$ and radii of curvature $R_1$ and $R_2$. Let $O$ be the optical centre.

**Step 1 — First refraction at surface $AP_1B$:**

A point object at $O$ (distance $u$ from $P_1$) is imaged at $I_1$ (distance $v_1$). Using the refraction formula at a single spherical surface,

$$\frac{n_2}{v_1}-\frac{n_1}{u}=\frac{n_2-n_1}{R_1}\quad\text{... (1)}$$

**Step 2 — Second refraction at surface $AP_2B$:**

The image $I_1$ acts as the object for the second surface, at distance $v_1$ (virtual object, but for a thin lens $P_1\approx P_2$, so the object distance is $v_1$). The final image is formed at $I$ at distance $v$:

$$\frac{n_1}{v}-\frac{n_2}{v_1}=\frac{n_1-n_2}{R_2}\quad\text{... (2)}$$

**Step 3 — Add (1) and (2):**

$$\frac{n_1}{v}-\frac{n_1}{u}=(n_2-n_1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$

**Step 4 — For an object at infinity** ($u=\infty$), the image forms at the focus, $v=f$. Hence

$$\boxed{\frac{1}{f}=\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_2}\right)}$$

which is the lens maker's formula. For a lens in air ($n_1=1$, $n_2=n$): $\dfrac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.
